title: Trunk Wall: Ribs, Diaphragm & Abdominal Wall
summary: Understand the muscular and skeletal walls that enclose the thorax and abdomen, and how nerves and vessels travel within them.

lessons.title: The Thoracic Cage: Ribs, Sternum and Costovertebral Joints

levels.kid:
Put your hands on your chest and take a deep breath. Feel it get bigger? Under your skin is a bony cage called the **rib cage**.

It is made of 12 pairs of curved bones called **ribs**. In the back, they join your spine. In the front, most of them join a flat bone in the middle of your chest called the **sternum**, or breastbone.

The cage is like a helmet for your heart and lungs. But it is not stiff like a real helmet. The front parts of the ribs are bendy **cartilage**, a bit like the tip of your nose. Little joints in the back let the ribs swing up and out, like bucket handles, so your lungs have room to fill with air.
levels.hs:
The **thoracic cage** is the bony and cartilaginous framework of the chest. It protects the heart, lungs and great vessels, gives muscles places to attach, and moves during breathing.

Its parts:
- **12 thoracic vertebrae** at the back.
- **12 pairs of ribs**. Ribs 1-7 are **true ribs** because each one's cartilage attaches directly to the sternum. Ribs 8-10 are **false ribs** because their cartilages join the cartilage above. Ribs 11-12 are **floating ribs** with free front ends.
- **Costal cartilages**, which are bars of hyaline cartilage that add flexibility.
- The **sternum**, made of three parts: the **manubrium** at the top, the **body**, and the small **xiphoid process** at the bottom.

The manubrium and body meet at the **sternal angle** (angle of Louis), a ridge you can feel. Rib 2 attaches there, so clinicians use it to count ribs. It also lines up with the disc between vertebrae T4 and T5.

At the back, each rib forms joints with the spine. These are the **costovertebral joints**. They let ribs rotate. This creates two movements. The upper ribs lift the sternum forward, called the **pump-handle** movement. The lower ribs swing outward, called the **bucket-handle** movement. Both make the chest larger so air flows in.

Real example: in CPR, compressions on the lower sternum work because the flexible cage lets the chest be pushed down and spring back.
levels.college:
**Typical ribs (3-9)** have a **head** with two demifacets, a **neck**, a **tubercle**, and a **shaft** with an **angle** and an inferior **costal groove**. The head's superior demifacet joins the vertebra above, and its inferior demifacet joins its own vertebra. For example, rib 6 joins T5 and T6.

**Atypical ribs**:
- **Rib 1**: shortest, broadest and most curved. Its single facet joins T1. Its superior surface has the **scalene tubercle** for anterior scalene, with grooves for the subclavian vein in front and the subclavian artery behind.
- **Rib 2**: thinner, with a tuberosity for serratus anterior.
- **Ribs 10-12**: a single head facet. Ribs 11-12 have no neck or tubercle.

**Costovertebral joints** are synovial and come in two kinds:
- **Joint of the head**: an intra-articular ligament anchors the crest of the head to the intervertebral disc. The radiate ligament reinforces it.
- **Costotransverse joint**: the tubercle meets the transverse process of its own vertebra. Costotransverse ligaments reinforce it. Ribs 11-12 lack this joint.

**Sternal joints**:
- **Manubriosternal joint**: a secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis) at the sternal angle. It often ossifies in later life.
- **Xiphisternal joint**: lies at about T9.
- **Sternocostal joints**: the first is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis). Joints 2-7 are synovial.
- **Costochondral joints** are primary cartilaginous. **Interchondral joints** (cartilages 6-9) are synovial.

**Mechanics**: the axis through the head and tubercle sets the direction of rib movement. Upper costotransverse facets are cupped, so ribs rotate about that axis. This raises the sternum forward, increasing anteroposterior diameter (pump handle). Lower facets are flat, so ribs glide and rise laterally, increasing transverse diameter (bucket handle).

The **superior thoracic aperture** (T1, rib 1, manubrium) is clinically called the thoracic outlet. The **inferior aperture** is closed by the diaphragm.
levels.phd:
**Ossification and development.** Ribs arise from the costal processes of thoracic sclerotome. Hox genes regulate their segmental identity: Hox10 paralogs repress rib formation in the lumbar region, and Hox6 helps specify thoracic identity. Ribs ossify from a primary centre in the shaft, plus secondary centres for the head and tubercle that fuse around 20-25 years. The sternum forms from paired **sternal bars** of lateral plate mesoderm that fuse in the midline in a craniocaudal direction. Incomplete fusion can produce a **sternal foramen**, usually in the lower body, or a sternal cleft. This matters because an unrecognized foramen sits directly over the pericardium during sternal needle procedures.

**Joint biomechanics.** The rib neck axis runs roughly coronal in the upper ribs and becomes more sagittal in the lower ribs. This geometry, together with the facet shape, decides whether rotation mainly lifts the sternum (anteroposterior expansion) or swings the shaft laterally (transverse expansion). The **costal cartilages** store torsional energy during inspiration. Their elastic recoil helps quiet expiration. With age, cartilage calcification and ossification of the manubriosternal joint stiffen the cage and reduce chest-wall compliance. This partly explains the fall in respiratory system compliance in the elderly.

**Mechanical failure.** Ribs tend to break at the angle or the posterolateral shaft, where curvature concentrates stress. A **flail segment** forms when 3 or more adjacent ribs each break in 2 or more places. The segment moves paradoxically, sucking inward during inspiration. Older teaching blamed hypoxia on the paradoxical movement itself, but much of the harm comes from the underlying pulmonary contusion and pain-limited ventilation.

**Variation.** **Cervical ribs**, usually from C7, occur in roughly 0.5-1% of people, and many are asymptomatic. They are linked to neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome. A fibrous band from an incomplete cervical rib can compress the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1). Bifid (forked) ribs, lumbar ribs and fused ribs also occur. **Pectus excavatum** (sunken chest) and **pectus carinatum** (pigeon chest) reflect disordered costal cartilage growth. Their cause remains debated, with mechanical overgrowth and genetic connective-tissue factors both proposed.
levels.expert:
**Surface landmarks in practice.** The sternal angle is the most reliable starting point for counting ribs. Counting from the costal margin is error-prone because the floating ribs are hard to feel. Wrong-level rib or spine surgery remains a recognized never-event. When imaging is used to localize a level, confirm the count from T1/rib 1 and the twelfth rib, since a cervical rib or a hypoplastic twelfth rib can shift the count. Radiologists see this pitfall often in rib-fracture reporting.

**Imaging.** Plain radiographs miss a large share of rib fractures, especially anterior and cartilaginous ones. CT with 3D reconstruction is now the standard in significant trauma. Costal cartilage fractures appear on CT only indirectly unless the cartilage is calcified. Point-of-care ultrasound can detect cortical breaks and costochondral separation at the bedside.

**Surgical access.** **Median sternotomy** splits the sternum vertically. Surgeons close it with steel wires or plates. Sternal dehiscence and deep sternal wound infection (mediastinitis) are its main risks, and risk factors include diabetes and bilateral internal thoracic artery harvest. In children, sternotomy affects later cage growth less than early wide resection of costal cartilage. Older open pectus repair caused acquired asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy, which is why minimally invasive Nuss bar repair took over.

**Recent advances.** **Surgical stabilization of rib fractures (SSRF)** with precontoured plates is increasingly used for flail chest. Trials and meta-analyses suggest shorter ventilation and ICU stay in selected patients. Debate continues about non-flail multiple fractures. Regional techniques such as erector spinae and serratus anterior plane blocks are now widely used to control pain from rib fractures without central neuraxial access.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** The costotransverse joints and rib heads are a corridor to the thoracic spine. **Costotransversectomy** removes the medial rib and transverse process. This gives lateral access to ventral thoracic disc herniations and tumours without opening the chest. The rib head is an important landmark here, because it leads directly to the disc space of the same-numbered level.

**Open questions.** How costal cartilage ages, why pectus deformities progress during growth spurts, and the best threshold for SSRF remain active research areas.

In the next lesson, the spaces between the ribs and the structures that run within them are covered.

keyPoints: 12 rib pairs: true (1-7), false (8-10), floating (11-12)
Sternum = manubrium, body, xiphoid process
Sternal angle marks rib 2 and the T4/T5 level
Typical rib heads join two vertebrae plus a disc; tubercles join transverse processes
Upper ribs move like a pump handle, lower ribs like a bucket handle
Flail chest, cervical ribs and pectus deformities are key clinical links

test.q: Which ribs are classified as true ribs?
test.explain: Ribs 1-7 attach to the sternum directly through their own costal cartilages. Ribs 8-10 are false ribs and 11-12 are floating ribs.

test.q: Rib 2 articulates with the sternum at which landmark?
test.explain: Rib 2 meets the sternum at the sternal angle (angle of Louis). This makes the sternal angle the standard starting point for counting ribs.

test.q: The head of a typical rib 6 articulates with:
test.explain: A typical rib head joins the vertebra above (superior demifacet) and its own vertebra (inferior demifacet). Its tubercle, not its head, meets the transverse process.

test.q: The pump-handle movement mainly increases which chest dimension?
test.explain: The upper ribs raise the sternum forward and up, which deepens the chest front to back. The lower ribs' bucket-handle movement widens it side to side.

test.q: Which structure crosses the superior surface of rib 1 just behind the scalene tubercle?
test.explain: The groove behind the scalene tubercle carries the subclavian artery, while the vein runs in front of the tubercle.

test.q: What type of joint is the manubriosternal joint?
test.explain: It is a symphysis, which is a secondary cartilaginous joint, and it often ossifies with age. The first sternocostal joint is the primary cartilaginous one.

test.q: Which ribs lack a costotransverse joint?
test.explain: Ribs 11-12 have no neck or tubercle, so they do not articulate with transverse processes.

test.q: The sternal angle lies at the level of which intervertebral disc?
test.explain: The sternal angle lines up with the T4/T5 disc. The xiphisternal joint lies lower, at about T9.

test.q: A flail segment is defined as:
choices: One rib broken in three places
A fracture of the sternum body
Three or more ribs each broken twice
test.explain: A flail segment forms when 3 or more adjacent ribs each break in 2 or more places. The freed segment then moves paradoxically during breathing.

test.q: What is the lowest, smallest part of the sternum called?
test.explain: The sternum is made of the manubrium, the body, and the xiphoid process at the bottom.

test.q: Ribs 11 and 12 are called ___ ribs because their front ends are free.
test.explain: Ribs 11 and 12 do not attach to the sternum or to cartilages above, so their anterior ends are free.

test.q: The uppermost part of the sternum is the ___.
test.explain: The manubrium is the top part of the sternum and joins the body at the sternal angle.

kidTest.q: How many pairs of ribs do most people have?
kidTest.explain: Most people have 12 pairs of ribs, making 24 ribs in total.

kidTest.q: What does the rib cage protect?
kidTest.explain: The rib cage works like a helmet for the heart and lungs.

kidTest.q: What is the flat bone in the middle of your chest?
kidTest.explain: The sternum is the breastbone, and most ribs join it at the front.

kidTest.q: Why can your chest get bigger when you breathe in?
choices: The ribs fall off for a moment
The ribs swing up and out
kidTest.explain: Joints at the back let the ribs swing up and out, like bucket handles, which gives the lungs room to fill.

kidTest.q: The bendy front parts of the ribs are made of c _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cartilage is bendy tissue, like the tip of your nose, and it lets the rib cage flex.

advancedTest.q: During a costotransversectomy, why is the rib head a useful landmark?
choices: It marks where the phrenic nerve exits the canal
It overlies the spinal cord exactly at its own level
It leads to the disc space of the same-numbered level
It lies directly over the vertebral artery origin
advancedTest.explain: The rib head attaches to the disc, so following it leads directly to the disc space of the same-numbered level. This is how surgeons reach ventral thoracic pathology.

advancedTest.q: A rib count started from the costal margin places a lesion one level off. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The xiphoid process often hides rib 7 from touch
Hard-to-feel floating ribs or variant ribs
The sternal angle varies widely between patients
Ribs 8-10 attach to the sternum in many adults
advancedTest.explain: The floating ribs are hard to palpate, and a cervical rib or hypoplastic twelfth rib can shift a count. That is why counting should be confirmed from rib 1 and rib 12, or from the sternal angle.

advancedTest.q: Why do lower ribs expand the chest mainly in transverse diameter?
choices: They lack costal cartilages along their length
Their necks are shorter than the necks of upper ribs
Their axes are more sagittal and their facets flatter
They are fused to the diaphragm at the angle
advancedTest.explain: A more sagittal neck axis and flat costotransverse facets let the lower ribs glide and swing laterally. This creates the bucket-handle movement.

advancedTest.q: Current understanding of hypoxia in flail chest emphasizes:
choices: Underlying lung contusion and pain-limited ventilation
Compression of the phrenic nerve by bone fragments
Paradoxical motion as the main cause of hypoxia
advancedTest.explain: Older teaching blamed the paradoxical movement itself. Much of the harm actually comes from pulmonary contusion and from ventilation limited by pain.

lessons.title: Intercostal Spaces and the VAN Neurovascular Bundle

levels.kid:
Your ribs are like the bars of a birdcage that protects your heart and lungs. But the gaps between the bars are not empty! Each gap is filled with thin layers of muscle, like a sandwich with three slices.

Tucked under the bottom edge of each rib is a tiny groove, like a hidden tunnel. Inside it run three neighbors: a **vein**, an **artery** and a **nerve**. Doctors remember their order from top to bottom with the word **VAN**, like a little van driving under each rib.

Because these tubes hide under the rib above, doctors who need to put a needle between ribs aim just above a rib, not just below one. That keeps the van safe!
levels.hs:
The **intercostal spaces** are the gaps between neighboring ribs. There are 11 on each side, and each is named for the rib above it, so the 5th intercostal space lies below rib 5.

Each space is filled by three thin layers of muscle:
- **External intercostals**: outermost; fibers run down and forward, like hands in your front pockets. They help lift the ribs when you breathe in.
- **Internal intercostals**: middle layer; fibers run at right angles to the externals. They help with forced breathing out.
- **Innermost intercostals**: the deepest, thinnest layer.

Between the internal and innermost layers runs the **neurovascular bundle**: an intercostal vein, artery and nerve. They sit in the **costal groove** on the lower inside edge of each rib, in the order **V-A-N** (vein, artery, nerve) from top to bottom.

This matters in real medicine. When doctors drain fluid or air from the chest (for example, a **chest tube** for a collapsed lung), they insert the needle or tube just above the upper border of the rib below. This avoids the bundle hiding under the rib above. Damaging the artery could cause serious bleeding, and hitting the nerve causes pain.

The intercostal nerves also supply the skin of the chest. Shingles, a reactivated chickenpox virus, often causes a painful rash in a band following one of these nerves.
levels.college:
**Layers of an intercostal space** (superficial to deep):
- **External intercostal**: fibers pass inferomedially (down and forward), running from the tubercles of the ribs back to near the costochondral junctions. Anteriorly it is replaced by the **external intercostal membrane**. It acts in inspiration.
- **Internal intercostal**: fibers pass inferolaterally, running from the sternum to the angles of the ribs. Posteriorly it becomes the **internal intercostal membrane**. Its interosseous part aids forced expiration; the interchondral part near the sternum aids inspiration.
- **Innermost intercostal**: continuous in the same plane with the **subcostals** (posteriorly) and **transversus thoracis** (anteriorly).
- Deep to these lie the **endothoracic fascia** and then the **parietal pleura**.

**The neurovascular bundle** runs in the plane between the internal and innermost intercostals, sheltered by the **costal groove**. Order from superior to inferior is **vein, artery, nerve**, so the nerve is the least protected. Small collateral branches run along the upper border of the rib below.

**Arterial supply**:
- **Posterior intercostal arteries**: spaces 1-2 from the **supreme (superior) intercostal artery** (costocervical trunk of the subclavian); spaces 3-11 from the **thoracic aorta**.
- **Anterior intercostal arteries**: from the **internal thoracic artery** (spaces 1-6) and its **musculophrenic** branch (spaces 7-9). The anterior and posterior vessels anastomose in each space.

**Venous drainage**: posteriorly to the **azygos** system (azygos on the right; hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos on the left), anteriorly to the internal thoracic veins.

**Nerves**: ventral rami of **T1-T11** are the intercostal nerves; T12 is the **subcostal nerve**. Each gives lateral and anterior cutaneous branches supplying a **dermatome**. T7-T11 continue as **thoracoabdominal nerves** into the abdominal wall.

**Clinical rule**: insert needles and chest drains just above the rib below.
levels.phd:
The intercostal space is a segmental unit: each preserves the body-wall plan inherited from somites. Its muscles derive from the **hypaxial** dermomyotome and are innervated by ventral rami. They correspond layer for layer with the three anterolateral abdominal muscles: external intercostal with external oblique, internal intercostal with internal oblique, innermost intercostal with transversus abdominis. The neurovascular plane between the second and third layers continues into the abdomen between internal oblique and transversus abdominis. The **transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block** exploits exactly this.

**Respiratory mechanics.** The classic Hamberger model held that external intercostals elevate ribs because their fibers form a lever acting on the lower rib. De Troyer and colleagues refined this with electromyography and measured mechanical advantage. Inspiratory effect is greatest in the dorsal, upper spaces and declines ventrally and caudally. The **parasternal (interchondral) intercostals** are obligatory inspiratory muscles active in quiet breathing. Expiratory internal intercostal activity is largest in the lower, lateral spaces. Activity is thus topographically graded by mechanical advantage, not simply sorted by layer.

**Vascular variation.** Text order (VAN) holds well at the costal groove, but cadaveric and CT angiographic studies show the posterior intercostal artery is tortuous and exposed near the vertebral column. Medial to the rib angle, the artery often lies mid-space before entering the groove. Tortuosity increases with age, so the "safe triangle" logic weakens posteriorly. The anastomoses between aortic intercostals and the internal thoracic system become **collateral pathways in aortic coarctation**. The enlarged, pulsatile intercostals erode the inferior rib margins, producing **rib notching** (Roesler sign) on radiographs, typically of ribs 3-8. Ribs 1-2 are spared because their arteries come from the costocervical trunk.

**Neural detail.** Each intercostal nerve gives a collateral branch, a lateral cutaneous branch near the midaxillary line (dividing into anterior and posterior twigs) and an anterior cutaneous branch. Part of T1 joins the brachial plexus. The **intercostobrachial nerve** (lateral cutaneous of T2) supplies the medial upper arm, which explains arm pain referred from thoracic sources. Adjacent dermatomes overlap substantially, so loss of one intercostal nerve rarely produces complete anesthesia.
levels.expert:
**Procedural safety.** Guidance for pleural procedures (for example, BTS pleural guidelines) recommends the **triangle of safety**: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, and a line at the level of the nipple (about the 5th space), with the apex below the axilla. Insertion goes over the superior border of the rib below. Ultrasound guidance is now standard and reduces complications. Ultrasound with colour Doppler can directly visualise an exposed intercostal artery, which matters most in elderly patients and in posterior approaches. Intercostal artery injury is a recognised cause of **haemothorax** after thoracentesis or drain placement. It may present late and can require angiographic embolisation or surgery.

**Regional anaesthesia.** Intercostal nerve blocks target the nerve near the rib angle, before the lateral cutaneous branch arises. Systemic absorption from intercostal injection is among the highest of the peripheral blocks because the space is so vascular, so local anaesthetic toxicity is a real concern. Fascial plane blocks have largely displaced multilevel intercostal injections for thoracic and breast surgery: the **paravertebral**, **erector spinae plane** and **serratus anterior plane** blocks, and **PECS** blocks. Their mechanisms of spread, and their efficacy relative to paravertebral and epidural techniques, remain debated.

**Pain syndromes.** Post-thoracotomy pain syndrome affects a substantial minority of patients. It is attributed largely to intercostal nerve injury from rib retraction, compression by pericostal sutures and rib fracture. This has motivated **intracostal suturing**, muscle-sparing incisions, VATS/robotic approaches and **intercostal nerve cryoablation**, which is increasingly used in Nuss repair of pectus excavatum. Post-herpetic neuralgia follows thoracic dermatomes most often. **Slipping rib syndrome**, involving hypermobile ribs 8-10, irritates intercostal nerves.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Intercostal nerves serve as donors in **nerve transfers** for brachial plexus avulsion, for example intercostal-to-musculocutaneous transfer to restore elbow flexion. The thoracic dermatomes provide sensory levels for localising spinal cord lesions: T4 lies at the nipple and T10 at the umbilicus. The intercostal space is also the corridor for thoracoscopic anterior spinal approaches.

**Open questions** include predicting artery position in individual patients, and long-term outcomes of cryoablation, including the risk of neuropathic pain after nerve regrowth.

keyPoints: 11 intercostal spaces per side, each named for the rib above
Three muscle layers: external, internal and innermost intercostals
The neurovascular bundle runs between the internal and innermost layers in the costal groove
Order top to bottom: vein, artery, nerve (VAN)
Posterior intercostal arteries come from the aorta; anterior ones come from the internal thoracic artery
Insert needles and chest drains just above the rib below

test.q: From superior to inferior in the costal groove, the bundle's order is:
test.explain: VAN: vein highest, then artery, then nerve, which is the least protected.

test.q: The intercostal neurovascular bundle runs between which muscle layers?
test.explain: The bundle lies in the plane between the internal and innermost intercostals.

test.q: Where should a chest drain be inserted relative to the ribs?
choices: Over the upper border of the rib below
Through the middle of a rib
test.explain: Going over the rib below avoids the main bundle sheltered under the rib above.

test.q: Posterior intercostal arteries of spaces 3-11 arise from the:
test.explain: The aorta supplies spaces 3-11; spaces 1-2 are supplied from the supreme intercostal artery via the costocervical trunk.

test.q: Anterior intercostal arteries of spaces 1-6 branch from the:
test.explain: The internal thoracic artery gives the anterior intercostals of spaces 1-6; its musculophrenic branch supplies spaces 7-9.

test.q: Fibers of the external intercostal muscle run:
test.explain: External intercostal fibers run inferomedially, like hands in front pockets; the internal layer runs at right angles.

test.q: Posterior intercostal veins on the right drain mainly into the:
test.explain: On the right they drain to the azygos vein; on the left they drain to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins.

test.q: The 5th intercostal space lies:
test.explain: Each space is named for the rib above it, so the 5th space lies between ribs 5 and 6.

test.q: A band-shaped shingles rash on the chest follows a:
test.explain: Shingles reactivates within one sensory nerve and spreads along the strip of skin that nerve supplies.

test.q: The ventral ramus of T12 is called the ___ nerve.
test.explain: T12 lies below the 12th rib, so it is subcostal, not intercostal.

test.q: What is the groove on the lower inner edge of each rib that shelters the bundle called?
test.explain: The costal groove protects the vein and artery best; the nerve is the lowest and most exposed.

test.q: Intercostal nerves T7-T11 continue into the abdominal wall as ___ nerves.
test.explain: These nerves supply both the chest wall and the abdominal wall.

kidTest.q: What fills the gaps between your ribs?
kidTest.explain: Three thin muscle layers fill each gap.

kidTest.q: Where does the little tunnel for the vein, artery and nerve hide?
kidTest.explain: It sits in a groove under the bottom edge of each rib.

kidTest.q: Where do doctors aim a needle between ribs?
kidTest.explain: Aiming just above a rib keeps the needle away from the tubes hiding under the rib above.

kidTest.q: What do your ribs protect?
kidTest.explain: The rib cage guards your heart and lungs.

kidTest.q: The word that helps you remember vein, artery, nerve: v _ _
kidTest.explain: VAN stands for vein, artery, nerve, from top to bottom.

advancedTest.q: In coarctation of the aorta, why are ribs 1-2 typically spared from notching?
choices: Their costal grooves are absent, so dilated arteries have nothing to erode
The internal thoracic artery is occluded at these levels in coarctation
Their arteries drain into the azygos system rather than forming anastomoses
Their intercostal arteries arise above the coarctation, from the costocervical trunk
advancedTest.explain: Spaces 1-2 are supplied from the supreme intercostal artery, not the aorta, so their vessels do not enlarge as collaterals.

advancedTest.q: Why is VAN-based 'over the rib below' guidance least reliable posteriorly near the spine?
choices: The intercostal nerve lies above the vein there and blocks the route
The pleura is absent near the vertebral bodies, so there is no target
The artery is tortuous and may lie mid-space before entering the groove
The intercostal muscle layers fuse and lose their separate fascial planes
advancedTest.explain: Medial to the rib angle the artery is often exposed and mid-space, especially with age, so it may lie in the needle's path.

advancedTest.q: A TAP block reaches the abdominal wall nerves because that plane corresponds to which thoracic plane?
advancedTest.explain: The internal oblique/transversus plane is the abdominal continuation of the internal/innermost intercostal neurovascular plane.

advancedTest.q: EMG studies by De Troyer suggest intercostal respiratory action is best explained by:
choices: Phrenic innervation that spreads into intercostal muscle
Layer alone, so external layers inspire and internal layers expire
Regional mechanical advantage that varies by location
Equal activity of each space with each breath
advancedTest.explain: Inspiratory and expiratory effects vary by location (dorsal-upper versus lower-lateral), and the parasternal internal intercostals are inspiratory. This refines the simple layer-based Hamberger model.

lessons.title: The Diaphragm: Structure, Openings and Phrenic Innervation

levels.kid:
Under your lungs is a big, dome-shaped muscle called the **diaphragm**. It looks a bit like an upside-down bowl or the top of a jellyfish.

When you breathe in, the diaphragm squeezes and flattens. That makes more room in your chest, so air rushes into your lungs, like pulling the handle of a pump. When it relaxes, it goes back up and air flows out.

The diaphragm has a few holes in it, like doors in a wall. Your food tube and some big blood vessels pass through these doors.

A special nerve called the **phrenic nerve** tells the diaphragm when to move. A hiccup happens when the diaphragm jumps suddenly!
levels.hs:
The **diaphragm** is a thin, dome-shaped sheet of muscle that separates the **thoracic cavity** (chest) from the **abdominal cavity** (belly). It is the main muscle of breathing.

Its structure has two parts:
- **Muscle fibers** around the edge, attached to the lower ribs, the bottom of the sternum, and the lumbar vertebrae.
- A tough, flat sheet of tendon in the middle called the **central tendon**. The heart sits on top of it.

When the muscle contracts, the domes flatten and move down. Chest volume increases, pressure inside drops, and air is drawn into the lungs. This is **inspiration**. Quiet breathing out is mostly passive: the diaphragm relaxes and rises.

Three major structures pass through it. A classic memory trick is "**I 8 10 Eggs At 12**":
- **IVC** (inferior vena cava) at the level of vertebra **T8**
- **Esophagus** at **T10**
- **Aorta** at **T12**

The diaphragm is controlled by the **phrenic nerves**, one on each side. They come from spinal nerves **C3, C4 and C5** in the neck. Students remember this with "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive."

Real example: a high neck injury above C3 can stop the diaphragm from working, so the person needs a ventilator to breathe.
levels.college:
The diaphragm is a musculotendinous partition with a right dome (higher, pushed up by the liver) and a left dome. At full expiration the right dome reaches about the 5th rib or intercostal space.

**Muscular origins** converge on the **central tendon**:
- **Sternal part**: slips from the back of the xiphoid process.
- **Costal part**: inner surfaces of the lower six costal cartilages and ribs.
- **Lumbar part**: the **right and left crura** (right from L1–L3, left from L1–L2) plus the **medial and lateral arcuate ligaments**, which arch over psoas major and quadratus lumborum.

The crura join in front of the aorta as the **median arcuate ligament**.

**Major openings**:
- **Caval foramen (T8)**: in the central tendon. It carries the IVC and branches of the right phrenic nerve. Inspiration stretches it open, which helps venous return.
- **Esophageal hiatus (T10)**: in the muscle of the right crus. It carries the esophagus and the vagal trunks. Crural fibers act as a sphincter that helps prevent reflux.
- **Aortic hiatus (T12)**: behind the median arcuate ligament, so it lies technically outside the diaphragm. It carries the aorta, the thoracic duct and often the azygos vein. Breathing does not compress it.

The splanchnic nerves pierce the crura. The sympathetic trunks pass behind the medial arcuate ligaments.

**Innervation**:
- **Phrenic nerve (C3–C5)**: all motor supply, plus sensation from the central part (diaphragmatic pleura and peritoneum).
- **Lower intercostal nerves (T6–T11) and subcostal nerve**: sensation from the peripheral rim only.

Because central diaphragmatic irritation travels by C3–C5, pain is **referred to the shoulder tip** (C4 dermatome). Examples are blood under the diaphragm or gallbladder inflammation.

**Blood supply**: pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries (from the internal thoracic), superior and inferior phrenic arteries.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the diaphragm is where cervical neurology, thoracic surgery and abdominal surgery overlap.

**Phrenic injury and assessment**
- Unilateral paralysis is often discovered as an **elevated hemidiaphragm**. Causes include cardiac surgery (cold injury or stretch), tumor invasion such as lung apex or mediastinal nodes, and interscalene brachial plexus blocks. Blocks reach the phrenic nerve so often because it lies on scalenus anterior.
- The fluoroscopic **sniff test** shows paradoxical upward motion. Diaphragm ultrasound, measuring excursion and thickening fraction, now often replaces it at the bedside and in the ICU.
- **Ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction** develops quickly with controlled ventilation. Proteolysis and atrophy appear in human biopsies (Levine et al., 2008, NEJM). This drives research into diaphragm-protective ventilation.

**Pacing and neuromodulation**
For high cervical spinal cord injury with intact phrenic motor neurons, **phrenic or diaphragm pacing** is an option. It works by direct phrenic electrodes or laparoscopic intramuscular electrodes. Pacing can reduce ventilator dependence in some patients. A key prerequisite is confirming that lower motor neurons are intact, using phrenic conduction studies. Injury at C3–C5 itself may destroy the phrenic nuclei and make pacing futile. This bears directly on neurosurgical decision-making.

**Hiatal and traumatic problems**
- **Sliding hiatal hernias** (type I) enlarge the esophageal hiatus. **Paraesophageal hernias** (types II–IV) risk volvulus. Repair includes crural approximation, but recurrence remains a persistent problem, and the value of mesh reinforcement is still debated.
- **Blunt traumatic rupture** is more often left-sided, because the liver buffers the right side. It is easily missed on initial imaging and may present years later with herniated bowel.

**Pitfalls**
- Shoulder-tip pain may be subdiaphragmatic, not musculoskeletal.
- The right dome normally sits higher. Left-sided elevation or contour loss deserves attention.
- Eventration, a thinned and weak muscle, can mimic paralysis or hernia.

**Open questions**
Open questions include the true mechanism of median arcuate ligament syndrome and who benefits from decompression. Others are the optimal ultrasound thresholds for predicting weaning, and how phrenic plasticity can be exploited. One example is acute intermittent hypoxia protocols that enhance phrenic output after partial cervical injury.

keyPoints: The diaphragm is the main muscle of inspiration; contraction flattens its domes
Muscle fibers from sternal, costal and lumbar (crural) parts insert on the central tendon
IVC passes at T8, esophagus at T10, aorta at T12 ('I 8 10 Eggs At 12')
Phrenic nerves (C3-C5) give all motor supply: 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'
Central diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip
Cervical innervation reflects the diaphragm's origin from the septum transversum

test.q: Which spinal nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
test.explain: The phrenic nerve arises from C3, C4 and C5. T6-T11 is tempting, but those intercostal nerves only give sensation to the diaphragm's rim.

test.q: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pass through the diaphragm?
test.explain: The IVC passes through the caval foramen at T8. The esophagus passes at T10 and the aorta at T12.

test.q: Besides the esophagus, what passes through the esophageal hiatus?
test.explain: The anterior and posterior vagal trunks travel with the esophagus. The thoracic duct and azygos vein go with the aorta.

test.q: What happens to the diaphragm during inspiration?
test.explain: Contraction pulls the domes down and flattens them. This increases chest volume and draws air in.

test.q: Why is the aortic hiatus not narrowed when the diaphragm contracts?
choices: It lies behind the median arcuate ligament
It is surrounded by the right crus muscle
It lies within the central tendon
It is located inside the costal part
test.explain: The aortic hiatus sits behind the median arcuate ligament, so it is technically outside the diaphragm. The caval foramen is the opening in the central tendon.

test.q: Gallbladder inflammation irritating the central diaphragm often causes pain felt in the:
test.explain: Central diaphragm sensation travels in the phrenic nerve (C3-C5). The pain is therefore referred to the C4 dermatome at the shoulder tip.

test.q: Why does the right dome of the diaphragm usually sit higher than the left?
test.explain: The liver lies under the right dome and pushes it higher. The heart actually rests on the central tendon.

test.q: Which part of the diaphragm forms a sphincter-like sling around the esophagus?
test.explain: Fibers of the right crus surround the esophageal hiatus. They act as an extrinsic sphincter that helps prevent reflux.

test.q: The lower intercostal nerves supply the diaphragm with:
choices: Motor fibers to the costal part
Sensory fibers to the central part
test.explain: The intercostal and subcostal nerves carry sensation from the peripheral rim only. The phrenic nerve supplies all motor fibers and central sensation.

test.q: The fibrous center of the diaphragm on which the heart rests is the central ___.
test.explain: All muscle fibers converge on the central tendon.

test.q: Name the large vessel that passes through the diaphragm at T12.
test.explain: The aorta passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, along with the thoracic duct.

test.q: The diaphragm's lumbar origins are two muscular legs called the right and left ___.
test.explain: The crura arise from the lumbar vertebrae. The right crus comes from L1-L3 and the left from L1-L2.

kidTest.q: What shape is the diaphragm?
kidTest.explain: It is dome-shaped, like an upside-down bowl or the top of a jellyfish.

kidTest.q: Where is the diaphragm?
kidTest.explain: It sits under the lungs, between the chest and the belly.

kidTest.q: What does the diaphragm help you do?
kidTest.explain: When it squeezes and flattens, air rushes into your lungs.

kidTest.q: What happens when the diaphragm jumps suddenly?
kidTest.explain: A sudden jump of the diaphragm makes a hiccup.

kidTest.q: The nerve that tells the diaphragm to move is the p _ _ _ _ _ _ nerve.
kidTest.explain: The phrenic nerve sends the signals that make the diaphragm move.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a complete spinal cord injury at C2 has intact phrenic motor neurons. Why might phrenic pacing work for this patient but not after destruction of the C3-C5 ventral horns?
choices: Pacing drives the lower motor neurons, which need to survive
Pacing depends on intact innervation of the crura
Pacing requires sensory feedback from the intercostal nerves
Pacing activates the preBötzinger complex directly
advancedTest.explain: Pacing drives the intact phrenic lower motor neuron pathway. If the phrenic nuclei are destroyed, the nerve and muscle degenerate and stimulation is futile.

advancedTest.q: What is the best explanation for why a muscle at the thoracoabdominal junction is supplied by cervical nerves?
choices: Intercostal nerves are too short to reach the central tendon
The vagus nerve redirects cervical fibers into the abdomen
Cervical nerves have more fatigue-resistant motor units
Its precursors form at cervical levels and descend, bringing their nerves
advancedTest.explain: The septum transversum and the myoblasts from cervical somites originate at C3-C5 levels. As they descend, they drag the phrenic nerves with them.

advancedTest.q: The mortality of Bochdalek congenital diaphragmatic hernia is mainly due to:
choices: Compression of the IVC at the caval foramen
Injury to the phrenic nerve at birth
advancedTest.explain: Abdominal organs in the chest impair lung development. The resulting hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension drive outcome, more than the hernia itself.

advancedTest.q: Crural fibers relax during swallowing while costal fibers expand the lower rib cage. What does this support?
choices: The diaphragm acts as a single uniform muscle
The crural and costal parts are functionally distinct
The costal part has little role in breathing
The crura are supplied by the vagus nerve instead
advancedTest.explain: Different attachments, motor pools and behaviours show that the two parts are functionally distinct. The crural part also acts as an extrinsic esophageal sphincter.

lessons.title: Anterolateral Abdominal Wall Muscles and the Rectus Sheath

levels.kid:
Your tummy has no bones in the front to protect it. Instead, it has a strong wall made of muscles stacked in layers, like a sandwich.

There are three flat muscles on each side. Their fibers run in different directions, like the layers of plywood. That crisscross makes the wall extra strong.

Down the middle are two long strap muscles called the **six-pack** muscles. They sit inside a tough sleeve, like a sword in a case. The sleeve is made from the flat ends of the side muscles.

These muscles help you sit up, twist, cough, sneeze and blow out birthday candles. They also hold your insides in place, like a living belt.
levels.hs:
The front and sides of the abdomen are protected by muscle, not bone. This is the **anterolateral abdominal wall**.

It has three flat muscles on each side, from outside in:
- **External oblique**: fibers run down and forward, like hands in your front pockets.
- **Internal oblique**: fibers run roughly at right angles to the external oblique, fanning up and forward.
- **Transversus abdominis**: fibers run horizontally, like a corset.

The three layers have fibers pointing in different directions, which makes the wall strong yet flexible, like plywood.

In the middle are two vertical muscles, the **rectus abdominis** (the "six-pack"). The bumps come from **tendinous intersections**, fibrous bands that cross each muscle. The flat muscles end in sheet-like tendons called **aponeuroses**. These wrap around the rectus to form the **rectus sheath**, then meet at a midline seam, the **linea alba** ("white line"), which runs from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis.

Functions: flexing and twisting the trunk, and raising pressure inside the abdomen to cough, vomit, give birth or empty the bladder and bowels. They also help push air out during forced breathing.

Example: surgeons often open the abdomen through the linea alba (a **midline laparotomy**). It is nearly bloodless because few vessels or nerves cross it.
levels.college:
**Layers** (superficial to deep): skin, superficial fascia (fatty **Camper's** and membranous **Scarpa's** layers), the three flat muscles, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, then parietal peritoneum.

**Flat muscles**
- **External oblique**: arises from the outer surfaces of ribs 5-12 and inserts into the linea alba, pubic tubercle and anterior iliac crest. Its free lower border, rolled under between the ASIS and pubic tubercle, is the **inguinal ligament**.
- **Internal oblique**: arises from the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral inguinal ligament, and inserts into the lower ribs and the aponeurosis.
- **Transversus abdominis**: arises from the internal surfaces of costal cartilages 7-12, the thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest and lateral inguinal ligament.

**Vertical muscles**
- **Rectus abdominis**: runs from the pubic crest and symphysis to costal cartilages 5-7 and the xiphoid. Its tendinous intersections attach to the anterior sheath only.
- **Pyramidalis** (absent in some people): a small triangle that tenses the linea alba.

**Rectus sheath**
- Above the **arcuate line** (about one-third of the way from umbilicus to pubis): the anterior layer is external oblique aponeurosis plus the anterior lamina of the internal oblique. The posterior layer is the posterior lamina of the internal oblique plus transversus.
- Below the arcuate line: all three aponeuroses pass anterior to the rectus. Only transversalis fascia lies behind it.
- Contents: rectus, pyramidalis, **superior and inferior epigastric vessels**, and the terminal ends of nerves T7-T12.

**Innervation**: thoracoabdominal nerves (T7-T11), the subcostal nerve (T12), and the iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1). These run between internal oblique and transversus. The dermatomes are T10 at the umbilicus and L1 at the groin.

**Lines**: the **linea semilunaris** marks the lateral rectus border. The superficial epigastric and superficial circumflex iliac vessels supply the superficial wall.
levels.phd:
The wall is a pressurized composite. Fiber angles of roughly ±45° in the two obliques plus 90° in transversus resemble a cross-ply laminate. This lets the wall resist intra-abdominal pressure in several directions while still allowing flexion and rotation. The aponeuroses are not simple sheets. Axer and colleagues described their collagen as multilayered and multidirectional, with fibers crossing the midline. This decussation makes the linea alba a true interweaving of the two sides rather than a weld between them. It explains why a midline wall resists stretching mainly across its width.

**Arcuate line nuance**: the line is often a gradual transition rather than a sharp edge. Its height varies, and it may be absent or doubled. Below it, the inferior epigastric artery runs on transversalis fascia and enters the sheath near the line.

**Vascular anatomy**: the **superior epigastric artery** (a terminal branch of the internal thoracic) joins the **inferior epigastric artery** (from the external iliac) within or behind the rectus through choke vessels. This forms a subclavian-to-external-iliac collateral that can bypass an obstructed aorta, as in coarctation or aortoiliac occlusion. Taylor's angiosome work showed that the inferior system is dominant, with **periumbilical perforators** concentrated near the umbilicus. This finding underpins perforator flap design.

**Neural anatomy**: the segmental nerves run in the **transversus abdominis plane**, between internal oblique and transversus, with segmental vessels. They pierce the posterior sheath near its lateral edge, run deep to the rectus, then send anterior cutaneous branches through it. The rectus is supplied in segments with little overlap. Cutting several adjacent nerves, for example with long vertical paramedian incisions, therefore denervates the medial muscle.

**Function**: transversus contracts early, before limb movement, a pattern described by Hodges and Richardson. This early contraction was proposed as feedforward spinal stabilization through tension in the thoracolumbar fascia. Its role in back pain is debated, and "core stability" treatment trials show modest, nonspecific benefits.

**Development**: the muscles form from hypaxial myotome cells that migrate in a ventral sheet. Failure of the wall to close contributes to omphalocele. Absent muscles with urinary tract anomalies define **prune belly (Eagle-Barrett) syndrome**.
levels.expert:
**Incisions and closure**: midline laparotomy avoids nerves but heals in avascular tissue. The incisional hernia rate approaches 10-20% in many series. The STITCH trial (Deerenberg, 2015) showed that a **small-bites** technique (5 mm stitches placed 5 mm apart, with a suture-to-wound length ratio of at least 4:1) lowers this rate compared with large bites. Lateral and transverse incisions damage the segmental nerves less. Even so, careless Kocher or paramedian incisions can cause **bulge from denervation**, which is easily mistaken for a hernia. Ultrasound or CT showing thinned muscle without a defect helps tell the two apart.

**Hernias**: **Spigelian hernias** pass through the linea semilunaris, usually below the arcuate line, where the posterior sheath is missing. They are often hidden under an intact external oblique aponeurosis and are easily missed on examination. **Diastasis recti**, a widened linea alba common after pregnancy, is not a hernia and carries no risk of strangulation.

**Abdominal wall reconstruction**: **component separation** releases layers so the rectus can be advanced to the midline.
- Anterior separation (Ramirez) divides the external oblique aponeurosis lateral to the semilunaris.
- **Transversus abdominis release** (TAR; Novitsky, 2012) works through a posterior route and creates a wide retromuscular plane for mesh.

What mesh to use (synthetic or biologic) and where to place it (onlay, sublay or intraperitoneal) remain debated. Sublay placement generally has the fewest recurrences.

**Hemorrhage**: **rectus sheath hematoma** arises from torn epigastric vessels, especially in older patients taking anticoagulants who cough hard. Below the arcuate line, bleeding can spread behind the rectus into the space of Retzius. **Carnett's sign** (pain persists or worsens when the wall is tensed) points to a source in the wall itself, such as hematoma or **anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment** (ACNES), rather than the viscera.

**Regional anesthesia**: TAP, rectus sheath and the newer quadratus lumborum and erector spinae plane blocks target the segmental nerves. TAP blocks cover the skin and muscle of the wall but not the viscera.

**Laparoscopy**: port sites near the lateral rectus border risk injuring the inferior epigastric artery. Seeing the vessel through the laparoscope, about 5 cm or more from the midline, avoids it.

**Flaps**: the deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flap now generally replaces the TRAM flap for breast reconstruction. It spares the rectus muscle, and mapping perforators with CT angiography before surgery shortens the operation.

keyPoints: Three flat muscles: external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis
Rectus abdominis lies in the rectus sheath formed by their aponeuroses
Below the arcuate line all aponeuroses pass anterior; only transversalis fascia lies behind
Linea alba is a midline aponeurotic seam from xiphoid to pubic symphysis
Nerves T7-L1 run between internal oblique and transversus (TAP plane)
Superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the sheath

test.q: Which is the deepest of the three flat abdominal muscles?
test.explain: From superficial to deep, the flat muscles are the external abdominal oblique, the internal abdominal oblique, and then the transversus abdominis. The rectus abdominis is a vertical muscle, not one of the flat layers.

test.q: The fibers of the external oblique run in which direction?
choices: Down and forward, like hands in pockets
Up and backward toward the spine
test.explain: External oblique fibers run inferomedially, like hands in front pockets. Horizontal fibers belong to transversus abdominis.

test.q: Below the arcuate line, what lies directly posterior to the rectus abdominis?
test.explain: Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass in front of the rectus. Only transversalis fascia lies behind it.

test.q: The transverse grooves that divide the 'six-pack' are produced by which structures?
test.explain: Fibrous tendinous intersections cross the rectus abdominis and adhere firmly to the anterior layer of the rectus sheath. This creates transverse grooves. The visible bulges are the muscle segments between them. The linea semilunaris forms a vertical, not transverse, groove at the lateral rectus border.

test.q: The inguinal ligament is formed by the lower border of which aponeurosis?
test.explain: The rolled-under free lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis, running from the ASIS to the pubic tubercle, forms the inguinal ligament.

test.q: Between which layers do the nerves of the abdominal wall mainly travel?
test.explain: The T7-L1 nerves run in the plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis, which is the target of TAP blocks.

test.q: The superior epigastric artery is a terminal branch of which artery?
test.explain: The superior epigastric comes from the internal thoracic artery. The inferior epigastric comes from the external iliac.

test.q: Why is a midline incision through the linea alba relatively bloodless?
choices: Few vessels or nerves cross the midline seam
Its fat layer absorbs bleeding from vessels
The rectus muscle covers it on both sides
It lies directly over the main aortic trunk
test.explain: The linea alba is an aponeurotic seam crossed by few vessels and nerves, so dividing it causes little bleeding or denervation.

test.q: Which dermatome lies at the level of the umbilicus?
test.explain: T10 supplies the skin around the umbilicus. L1 supplies the groin.

test.q: What midline 'white line' runs from the xiphoid process to the pubic symphysis?
test.explain: The linea alba is where the aponeuroses of both sides meet and interweave.

test.q: The curved line where the posterior rectus sheath ends below the umbilicus is the ___ line.
test.explain: Below the arcuate line all aponeuroses pass anterior to the rectus.

test.q: The lateral border of the rectus abdominis is marked by the linea ___.
test.explain: The linea semilunaris is the curved lateral edge of the rectus sheath.

kidTest.q: What protects the front of your tummy?
kidTest.explain: There are no bones in front of your tummy, so layers of muscle do the job.

kidTest.q: Why do the side muscle layers point in different directions?
choices: To make the wall extra strong
kidTest.explain: Crisscross layers make a strong wall, like plywood.

kidTest.q: The six-pack muscles sit inside a tough what?
kidTest.explain: They sit in a sleeve called the rectus sheath, like a sword in its case.

kidTest.q: Which of these do tummy muscles help you do?
kidTest.explain: Tummy muscles squeeze to help you cough, sneeze and sit up.

kidTest.q: Tummy muscles act like a living b _ _ _ that holds your insides in.
kidTest.explain: Like a belt, the muscles wrap around and hold everything in place.

advancedTest.q: A lateral bulge appears months after a long flank incision, yet CT shows thinned muscle and no fascial defect. The best explanation is:
choices: Rectus sheath hematoma spreading into the space of Retzius
Denervation of segmental nerves running in the transversus abdominis plane
A Spigelian hernia hidden beneath the external oblique aponeurosis
Diastasis recti caused by widening of the decussating linea alba
advancedTest.explain: Cutting segmental nerves paralyzes and thins the muscle, causing a bulge without any defect. A Spigelian hernia would show a defect at the linea semilunaris.

advancedTest.q: Why do Spigelian hernias occur mostly below the arcuate line?
choices: The internal oblique muscle is absent in the lower abdomen
The inferior epigastric artery weakens the fascia there
Rectus tendinous intersections are densest below the umbilicus
The posterior rectus sheath is absent there, leaving weaker support
advancedTest.explain: Below the arcuate line the posterior sheath is missing, leaving only transversalis fascia behind. This weakens the region near the linea semilunaris.

advancedTest.q: In aortic coarctation, blood can reach the legs through the rectus sheath mainly because of which connection?
choices: Thoracoabdominal nerves accompanied by segmental arteries
Superior epigastric joining inferior epigastric via choke vessels
Periumbilical perforators draining to the femoral vein
Superficial epigastric joining the superficial circumflex iliac
advancedTest.explain: The internal thoracic (from the subclavian) leads to the superior epigastric, which links to the inferior epigastric and then the external iliac, bypassing the narrowed aorta.

advancedTest.q: A TAP block gives good incision analgesia but the patient still reports deep visceral pain. Why?
choices: The block targets somatic wall nerves, not visceral afferents
The block reaches just the L1 ilioinguinal nerve
The local anesthetic spreads into the rectus sheath instead
Transversus abdominis is supplied by the phrenic nerve
advancedTest.explain: TAP blocks anesthetize the segmental somatic nerves of the wall. Visceral pain travels with autonomic afferents, which the block does not reach.

lessons.title: The Inguinal Canal: Walls, Rings and Contents

levels.kid:
Your belly has a strong wall made of muscle layers, like a stack of blankets. Low down, near the top of each leg, there is a tiny tunnel that slants through those layers. It is called the **inguinal canal**.

Why is there a tunnel? Before a baby boy is born, his testicles start inside his belly. They travel down through this tunnel to reach the outside. In girls, the tunnel holds a thin cord that helps hold the womb in place.

The tunnel has a door on the inside and a door on the outside. Because it slants, the muscles squeeze it shut when you cough or lift something. Sometimes a bit of gut pushes into the tunnel. That bulge is called a **hernia**, and surgeons can fix it.
levels.hs:
The **inguinal canal** is a passage about 4 cm long that runs through the lower front of the abdominal wall, just above the groin crease. It slopes downward, forward and toward the middle, running parallel to the **inguinal ligament**. The inguinal ligament is the folded lower edge of a flat muscle tendon that stretches from the hip bone to the pubic bone.

It has two openings:
- The **deep (internal) inguinal ring** is the inner entrance. It sits just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.
- The **superficial (external) inguinal ring** is the outer exit. It is a gap in the tendon of the external oblique muscle, just above the pubic tubercle.

What passes through it?
- In males, the **spermatic cord**. This bundle contains the **ductus (vas) deferens**, which carries sperm, along with the testicular artery and veins.
- In females, the **round ligament of the uterus**.
- In both sexes, the **ilioinguinal nerve**. It runs through the outer part of the canal and exits at the superficial ring.

The canal exists because the testes develop near the kidneys and move down into the scrotum before birth, pulling layers of the abdominal wall with them. The canal is a weak spot. An **inguinal hernia**, where abdominal contents bulge into the canal, is one of the most common reasons for surgery. It is much more common in males.
levels.college:
The inguinal canal is an oblique, roughly 4 cm intermuscular passage above the medial half of the inguinal ligament. It runs from the deep ring to the superficial ring.

**Rings**
- **Deep ring**: an opening in the **transversalis fascia**. It lies about 1-2 cm above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, just lateral to the **inferior epigastric vessels**.
- **Superficial ring**: a triangular defect in the **external oblique aponeurosis**, superolateral to the pubic tubercle. Its edges are the medial and lateral crura, held together by intercrural fibres.

**Walls** (mnemonic "MALT: 2Ms, 2As, 2Ls, 2Ts", read clockwise from superior)
- **Roof (superior)**: arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
- **Anterior**: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique.
- **Floor (inferior)**: the inguinal ligament, plus the **lacunar ligament** medially.
- **Posterior**: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the **conjoint tendon**.

**Contents**
- Spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of the uterus (female).
- **Ilioinguinal nerve** (L1). It enters through the side of the canal, not the deep ring, and runs outside the spermatic cord.
- The **genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve** runs within the cord and supplies the cremaster.

**Spermatic cord** contents include:
- the ductus deferens and its artery;
- the testicular artery;
- the **pampiniform venous plexus**;
- the cremasteric artery;
- autonomic fibres and lymphatics;
- the obliterated processus vaginalis.

The cord has three coverings, each derived from an abdominal wall layer. The **external spermatic fascia** comes from external oblique. The **cremasteric muscle and fascia** come from internal oblique. The **internal spermatic fascia** comes from transversalis fascia.

**Hernias**
- An **indirect** hernia enters the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
- A **direct** hernia pushes through the posterior wall medial to those vessels, within **Hesselbach's triangle**. The triangle's borders are the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral border of rectus abdominis, and the inguinal ligament.
levels.phd:
The canal is the developmental trace of testicular descent. The **gubernaculum**, a mesenchymal cord anchoring the gonad to the labioscrotal swelling, guides the testis in two phases. The **transabdominal phase** (around 8-15 weeks) depends on **INSL3** acting on its receptor **RXFP2** to swell the gubernaculum. The **inguinoscrotal phase** (around 25-35 weeks) is androgen-dependent and involves the genitofemoral nerve and CGRP signalling.

An evagination of peritoneum, the **processus vaginalis**, precedes the testis. It drags each abdominal wall stratum along, producing the layered coverings of the cord. External oblique contributes no muscle, only aponeurosis, so it yields fascia alone. Normally the processus vaginalis obliterates around birth, leaving the **tunica vaginalis** distally. Persistent patency explains:
- congenital **indirect hernias**;
- **communicating hydroceles**;
- **hydrocele of the canal of Nuck** in females, where the round ligament is the gubernacular homologue.

The canal's competence depends on two mechanisms, as classically described:
- **Obliquity**: rising intra-abdominal pressure presses the posterior wall against the anterior wall, flattening the canal like a valve.
- **Shutter mechanism**: contraction of internal oblique and transversus lowers the arching roof onto the floor. A sling of transversalis fascia at the deep ring is pulled upward and laterally, narrowing the ring.

For these reasons, where the walls lie relative to each ring matters. The anterior wall is strongest laterally, over the deep ring. The posterior wall is strongest medially, behind the superficial ring.

Two terms are often confused. The "conjoint tendon" is variably present as a true fusion of internal oblique and transversus aponeuroses; many dissections show separate insertions. The **falx inguinalis** is sometimes used as a synonym.

**Fruchaud's myopectineal orifice** unifies groin hernias as a single weak region. This bony-muscular frame is closed only by transversalis fascia and is divided by the inguinal ligament into an inguinal part and a femoral part. Indirect, direct and femoral hernias all emerge through it.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the canal is approached either anteriorly or posteriorly, and the posterior view changes the landmarks.

**Open anterior repair (Lichtenstein)**
The surgeon opens the external oblique aponeurosis, mobilises the cord and places a tension-free mesh on the posterior wall. Three nerves are at risk in the canal:
- the ilioinguinal nerve, lying on the cord;
- the iliohypogastric nerve, lying beneath the aponeurosis superiorly;
- the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, lying with the cremasteric vessels (the "blue line").

Nerve entrapment or injury drives **chronic postherniorrhaphy inguinal pain**. This affects roughly 10% of patients, with severe pain in a minority. Management options include identifying and preserving the nerves at operation, or planned neurectomy. Refractory cases may need triple neurectomy.

**Laparoscopic repair (TEP/TAPP)**
From inside, the surgeon sees the medial and lateral umbilical folds and the cord structures converging at the deep ring. Key danger zones are:
- the **triangle of doom**, between the vas deferens and gonadal vessels, which contains the external iliac vessels;
- the **triangle of pain**, lateral to the gonadal vessels and below the iliopubic tract, which contains the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and femoral nerve.

Tacks are avoided in both triangles. The **corona mortis**, an anastomosis between obturator and epigastric vessels crossing the superior pubic ramus, is a further bleeding hazard.

**Classification and imaging**
- European Hernia Society classification grades hernias as L (lateral/indirect), M (medial/direct) or F (femoral), with defect size.
- Dynamic ultrasound with Valsalva relies on the inferior epigastric vessels to label a hernia as direct or indirect.
- Intraoperatively, the direct-versus-indirect label rarely changes mesh choice. "Pantaloon" hernias straddle the vessels and occur in both compartments.

**Pitfalls**
- Femoral hernias lie below the inguinal ligament and are disproportionately common in women. They have a high strangulation risk, so they should not be dismissed as inguinal.
- **Sportsman's groin (inguinal disruption)** occurs without a true hernia and remains debated.
- The **watchful waiting** trials (Fitzgibbons) showed that minimally symptomatic men can safely defer repair, although most cross over to surgery within a decade.

Another open question concerns the biology of direct hernias: collagen type I/III imbalance suggests a connective tissue disorder rather than purely mechanical failure.

keyPoints: The inguinal canal is an oblique ~4 cm passage above the medial half of the inguinal ligament
Deep ring is in transversalis fascia; superficial ring is in external oblique aponeurosis
Walls: roof internal oblique/transversus, anterior external oblique, floor inguinal ligament, posterior transversalis fascia + conjoint tendon
Contents: spermatic cord or round ligament, plus the ilioinguinal nerve
Cord coverings come from external oblique, internal oblique (cremaster) and transversalis fascia
Indirect hernias are lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct hernias are medial, in Hesselbach's triangle

test.q: The deep inguinal ring is an opening in which layer?
test.explain: The deep ring is a gap in the transversalis fascia. The superficial ring is in the external oblique aponeurosis.

test.q: Which structure forms the floor of the inguinal canal?
test.explain: The inguinal ligament, with the lacunar ligament medially, forms the floor of the canal.

test.q: In a female, which structure travels through the inguinal canal?
test.explain: The round ligament of the uterus runs through the canal to the labium majus. The ovarian vessels do not use the canal.

test.q: The cremaster muscle in the spermatic cord comes from which wall layer?
test.explain: The cremasteric muscle and fascia derive from internal oblique. External oblique contributes the external spermatic fascia.

test.q: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal:
choices: Medial to the inferior epigastric vessels
test.explain: Indirect hernias pass through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. Direct hernias push through the posterior wall medial to them.

test.q: Which is NOT a border of Hesselbach's triangle?
test.explain: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral border of rectus abdominis and the inguinal ligament.

test.q: Which nerve runs in the canal but outside the spermatic cord?
test.explain: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) enters through the side of the canal, not the deep ring, and exits at the superficial ring outside the cord.

test.q: The posterior wall of the canal is reinforced medially by the:
test.explain: The conjoint tendon strengthens the posterior wall medially, behind the superficial ring.

test.q: Why does the inguinal canal exist?
choices: To carry the femoral artery to the thigh
To transmit the urethra to the perineum
Because the testes descend through the wall
To drain lymph from the lower limb
test.explain: Testicular descent, guided by the gubernaculum, creates the canal through the abdominal wall.

test.q: What is the duct in the spermatic cord that carries sperm?
test.explain: The ductus (vas) deferens carries sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra.

test.q: The venous network around the testicular artery in the cord is the ___ plexus.
test.explain: The pampiniform plexus is a network of veins within the spermatic cord.

test.q: The superficial inguinal ring lies just above the pubic ___.
test.explain: The superficial ring is located superolateral to the pubic tubercle.

kidTest.q: Where is the inguinal canal?
choices: In the middle of the back
Low on the belly, near the leg
kidTest.explain: It is a small tunnel low on the belly wall, near the top of the leg.

kidTest.q: What travels through the tunnel before a baby boy is born?
kidTest.explain: The testicles start inside the belly and move down through this tunnel.

kidTest.q: What holds the tunnel shut when you cough?
kidTest.explain: The tunnel slants, so the belly muscles squeeze it shut when you cough or lift.

kidTest.q: In girls, what is inside the tunnel?
kidTest.explain: In girls, the tunnel holds a thin cord that helps keep the womb in place.

kidTest.q: A bulge of gut pushing into the tunnel is a h _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A hernia happens when part of the gut pushes through a weak spot, and surgeons can fix it.

advancedTest.q: Why does external oblique contribute only fascia, not muscle, to the cord coverings?
choices: Its innervation is lost when the cord passes through
The processus vaginalis bypasses that layer during descent
The cord passes through it where it is purely aponeurotic
Its fibres degenerate during the transabdominal phase
advancedTest.explain: At the superficial ring, external oblique is aponeurosis. The coverings mirror the layer at each crossing point.

advancedTest.q: During laparoscopic repair, which area must be kept free of tacks to avoid injuring the external iliac vessels?
choices: Between the vas and gonadal vessels
The area lateral to the gonadal vessels
The space medial to the pubic tubercle
advancedTest.explain: The triangle of doom, between the vas and gonadal vessels, contains the external iliac vessels. The triangle of pain, lateral to the gonadal vessels, contains nerves.

advancedTest.q: A patent processus vaginalis in a newborn best explains which condition?
advancedTest.explain: When the processus vaginalis stays open, peritoneal fluid can reach the tunica vaginalis, producing a communicating hydrocele or an indirect hernia.

advancedTest.q: Strangulation risk aside, why can a femoral hernia be misdiagnosed as inguinal?
choices: Both pass through the deep inguinal ring
Both lie within the myopectineal orifice of Fruchaud
Both are supplied by the ilioinguinal nerve
Both lie lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels
advancedTest.explain: Fruchaud's orifice includes inguinal and femoral parts divided by the inguinal ligament. Femoral hernias emerge below the ligament but in the same weak region.
